subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for configuring the OAM identifiers that let MPLS and MPLS-TP paths be monitored.

tldr.problem: Operators of MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile networks need a standard way to configure the identifiers that OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) tools use to monitor tunnels, LSPs, pseudowires and sections.
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS-OAM-ID-STD-MIB module defines two tables: a Maintenance Entity Group (MEG) table and a Maintenance Entity (ME) table, plus a notification that fires when a MEG's operational status changes.
tldr.outcome: Managers can create and read OAM identifier configuration through SNMP, for both IP-compatible and ICC-based identifiers. The module sits at { mplsStdMIB 21 }.

today: RFC 7697 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2016. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFCs.

sections.title: Purpose and Context
sections.content:
RFC 7697 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. It describes managed objects for a Transport Profile based on MPLS, and is meant for OAM operations on MPLS tunnel LSPs, pseudowires and sections.

The RFC notes that SNMP SET is no longer recommended for configuring MPLS networks, as described in RFC 3812. Even so, some objects are read-write or read-create so that the module stays consistent with the base tables in RFC 3812. The configuration example in the RFC should be read as showing how values would appear when configured by other means.

The module is written in SMIv2 and fits the Internet-Standard Management Framework, in which objects are usually reached through SNMP.
sections.eli5: It is a standard list of settings that network gear can show or accept, so different makers' equipment speak the same language about monitoring.

sections.title: MEGs, MEs and Maintenance Points
sections.content:
The module supports OAM identifiers for point-to-point tunnels, point-to-multipoint LSPs, co-routed bidirectional LSPs, associated bidirectional LSPs and pseudowires. Both IP-compatible and ICC-based (ITU Carrier Code) identifier setups are covered, following RFC 6370.

A Maintenance Entity (ME) is a relationship between two points of a transport path, called Maintenance Entity Group End Points (MEPs), to which maintenance and monitoring apply. Between them there are zero or more Maintenance Entity Group Intermediate Points (MIPs). A Maintenance Entity Group (MEG) is a set of one or more MEs. MEPs and MIPs belong to the MEG and can be shared by more than one ME in it.
sections.eli5: Think of a relay race route. A group is the whole route, each leg is one entity, and the start and finish of a leg are its end points, with checkpoints in between.

sections.title: The MEG Table
sections.content:
The mplsOamIdMegTable manages one or more MEs that belong to the same transport path. Notable columns are:

  • mplsOamIdMegOperatorType: ipCompatible (1) or iccBased (2). ICC-based rows MUST have valid ICC and UMC values when the row is active.
  • mplsOamIdMegServicePointerType: tunnel, lsp, pseudowire or section, which says what kind of table entry the service pointer will point to.
  • mplsOamIdMegMpLocation: perNode (one MEP/MIP per LSR) or perInterface (two per LSR).
  • mplsOamIdMegPathFlow: unidirectional, co-routed bidirectional, associated bidirectional point-to-point, or unidirectional point-to-multipoint.

For an IP-compatible entry, the MEP_ID can be formed automatically as per RFC 6370. For an ICC-based path, the user is expected to configure the ICC identifier explicitly.
sections.eli5: The group table is where you describe the whole route: whose it is, what kind of path it follows, and which direction traffic goes.

sections.title: The ME Table and Operational Status
sections.content:
The mplsOamIdMeTable ties path information to a MEG. Each row has a name, an interface index, source and sink MEP indexes, a maintenance point type (mplsOamIdMeMpType, set to mep in the example), a MEP direction (mplsOamIdMeMepDirection) and a RowPointer to the first accessible column of the underlying path, such as an MPLS tunnel.

A MEG also reports status. mplsOamIdMegOperStatus is read-only and is up (1) or down (2). When it is down, at least one bit of mplsOamIdMegSubOperStatus is set to give the reason: megDown, meDown, oamAppDown or pathDown. The RFC says BFD is currently the only supported OAM application.

The notification mplsOamIdDefectCondition is sent whenever the operational status of the MEG changes. It carries the MEG name, the ME name, and both status objects.
sections.eli5: The second table describes each leg and its end points. A light shows green or red for the route, and extra flags say why it is red. When the light changes, the system sends an alert.

sections.title: Worked Example: A Co-routed Bidirectional LSP
sections.content:
The RFC walks through configuring OAM identifiers on a head-end LSR for a co-routed bidirectional LSP using IP-based identifiers. A MEG row is created with index 1, name MEG1, operator type ipCompatible, service pointer type lsp, MP location perNode and path flow coRoutedBidirectionalPointToPoint, using createAndGo (4) for the row status.

An ME row then links the path to that MEG: name ME1, source and sink MEP indexes of 0 because they are derived from the IP-compatible LSP, type mep, direction down, and a service pointer set to mplsTunnelName.1.1.10.20.
sections.eli5: The example fills in the two forms for one route: first the route itself, then a leg that points at the actual tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Improper manipulation of these objects may cause denial of service to a large number of end users. Read-write and read-create objects can be sensitive, and SET operations in a non-secure environment open devices to attack. Even readable objects may be sensitive: the two tables together show the MPLS OAM characteristics, so an administrator who wants to hide them should treat them as sensitive.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features. Those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy via the User-based Security Model with AES. It remains the operator's job to grant access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: These settings control how traffic flows, so only trusted people should be allowed to look at or change them, using a secure way of talking to the device.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: MPLS-related Standards Track MIB modules are rooted under the mplsStdMIB subtree. IANA assigned the object identifier { mplsStdMIB 21 } to the MPLS-OAM-ID-STD-MIB module. New assignments there can only be made through a Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The official registry gave this module its own address number, 21, in the MPLS part of the MIB tree.

items.text: The OAM application, currently only BFD, is down.

items.title: pathDown (3)
items.text: The underlying LSP or PW is down.
